_note: Every tunable number in the game. If a number appears in a .js file, it belongs here instead. Changing anything under 'climate', 'player.speed', or any site x/z means re-running the balance check.

world._scaleNote: One number for the size of the whole world. 1 is the nominal canyon: 600 m from end to end, 250 m across. Everything measured in metres multiplies by this at load. Deliberately NOT scaled: how fast you walk, how close you must stand to survey something, and anything vertical — you are the same size whatever the world does.
world._stripNote: The world is a STRIP: lengthX along the direction of travel, widthZ across it. size is the longer of the two for anything that still wants one number. segmentsX/segmentsZ are the terrain mesh's vertex grid — 4 m along the trail and 2 m across it, because the trail is only 7 m wide in the tunnels and a coarser grid across would render a seven-metre tunnel as two triangles.
world._sunNote: sunElevationDeg drives three things at once and they must not drift apart: where the DirectionalLight sits, where the sun is drawn, and how far rock throws its shadow. In a corridor running along x the side walls no longer shade anything — the sun is at +x, so what casts shade is every pass shoulder, every lateral offset in the chain, and the far end wall. A rib of height H shades H/tan(elev) metres of floor behind it: at 22 degrees that is 2.475*H. If you change this, re-run npm run balance and read the shaded percentage rather than guessing.

farHills._note: Silhouette only, and they must stay OUTSIDE the strip. The world is 2800 m long, so a ring at the old 2100 m put hills inside the corridor; minDistance is now past the far end. They are 82-99% fog by the time you see them.

scatterRocks._note: Loose rock, scattered. Cut hard when the world became a jungle: each of these is its own draw call, where the whole jungle is six, and a trail under closed canopy has very little bare rock showing.

palette._note: Ground colour, baked into the terrain mesh once at load. Costs nothing at runtime — change these freely. Each triple is r,g,b in 0..1. 'ash' is the flat ground, 'rock' is what steep slopes show, 'broadWarm' drifts the tone slowly across the map so large areas are not one flat colour.

path._note: THE TRAIL. A game trail through jungle, walked one way (+x). The herd tramples it through new growth every ninety days: that is why a path exists at all, why it runs the direction it runs, and why following it means following them. WHY +x, derived and not assumed: dawnX(t) = dawn0 + t*dawnVelocity with dawnVelocity positive, so the dawn line sweeps toward +x. Water arrives at dawn and growth is explosive and brief — the jungle comes up in the hours after the line passes, grows for one local day, and burns as the heat arrives. The player is walking inside that one day: ahead of them it is still coming up, behind them it is burning. There is no going back into the burn, which is the same one-way rule the rock had, wearing the right skin. NOTHING ELSE ENFORCES IT. Do not add anything that does.
path._shapeNote: TWO LAYERS still, and the reason is unchanged and measured. The OUTER wall is containment: its toe is a straight line at |z| = outerHalfWidth and nothing may make it depend on x, because a line that moves in the direction of travel is a diagonal ramp a flood fill will walk up. The INNER RIDGE is now a low bank of root mass and torn earth at the trail's edge rather than a cliff — ridgeTop is metres, not tens of metres — and what the player SEES as a wall is the vegetation standing on it (see the jungle block). The bank still does the containing, and it does it with ridgeLip: a discontinuity at the trail's edge that no stride can cross. THE PLAN IS BAKED into 1-D tables at `step` metres, so heightAt does one index and one lerp and the whole 2510 m trail costs less per call than a 600 m crevice did.
path._segmentNote: The chain, in order, walked from first to last. Alternate chamber and pass; the loader does not require it but the shape only reads if you do. length/halfWidth/centre are metres: length along x, halfWidth the TRAIL's half-width in z, centre its centreline in z. Tunnels are 7-9 m across, clearings 14-20 m. The `end` clearing is the widest at 20 m because the third grave sits 8 m off the centreline there and the beats are fixed. canopy is 0..1: how much of the sky this stretch has closed over, which is the shade mechanic — see the jungle block. Offsetting `centre` between consecutive segments is what stops you seeing the next chamber through a pass — a straight pass you can see down is not a pass. ridgeTop is how high the rock beside the floor stands above the local floor. THE FLOOR PROFILE, and this is where one-way comes from: a segment rises by `sill` over `sillRun` metres at its start, runs flat, falls by `drop` over `dropRun` metres, then runs flat for `dropTail` more. A smoothstep drop's steepest grade is 1.5*drop/dropRun; above player.maxClimbGrade that transition can be walked down and NOT back up, and the door has closed behind you. No script, no animation, no invisible wall — just ground. The sill also hides the next chamber's floor from this one. dropTail must be at least half of `blend` or the drop happens while the corridor is still changing shape, and a moving wall beside a drop is a ramp. POCKETS are the detours. A pocket hangs off ONE side of the corridor: `side` is -1 or +1 in z, `at` is where along the segment it centres (0..1), `length` how much of the journey it spans, `depth` how far it reaches off the main line, and `rise` how many metres of climb per metre of depth — a rise makes it a climb rather than a walk. `gives` is the finding that sits at its head, and it is documentation only: the site's real position is in config.sites. THE MAIN LINE IS SAFE FORWARD PROGRESS; the pockets are what cost time, and the dawn charges for time. That is the whole game.

segments.character: the trail comes out of the burn behind you; the growth here is already browning
seven metres of trail under closed canopy — the first place you cannot see ahead
close and dark; the undergrowth meets over the trail and you walk in green light
ONE-WAY: the trail drops off a root-bound step you cannot climb back
a clearing where the canopy has broken — the only sky on the route, and the sun gets in
ONE-WAY: the trail falls away under the closed canopy behind the handover
the herd has broken this stretch down; fallen trunks and torn ground
a tunnel, and a dead-end notch trampled off it
the ground steps up away from the trail on one side, growth climbing it
ONE-WAY: a long wet slope of trampled growth, walkable down and not up
low growth and standing water; the herd feeds through here and the sky is half open
a tunnel, and a notch that climbs away from it
the last clearing; the growth ahead has not come up yet

path._wallNote: The inner ridge. run is how far out from the floor's edge the ridge takes to reach its top; the talus pair is a short walkable scree apron then a SQUARE ROOT face, whose gradient at the toe is what stops you. Nothing here contains you — the outer wall does — so these numbers are free to be whatever reads best.
path._outerNote: The outer wall: containment, and the skyline behind the ridges. halfWidth is the fixed toe line — the one number in this file that must never be made to depend on x. crestY is an ABSOLUTE elevation, not a height above the floor, so the wall grows as the path descends. crestY must stay comfortably above the highest (segment base + ridgeTop) or the two layers cross.
path._endNote: The far end, closed. Same apron-then-square-root face as everything else.
path._floorNote: Ground detail, multiplied per segment by that segment's floorRelief. crossFall tips the floor across the corridor. The relief is terraced into benchSteps low benches with benchEdge as the fraction of a step the riser occupies — below about 0.5 the risers stop being walkable. All vertical, none of it touched by world.scale.
path._screeNote: Fallen material at the foot of the ridges, in props.js. Each piece finds the foot of the ridge at its x, measures how steep the rock above it is, and is kept with probability min(1, grade*steepBias)^steepPower — so the debris explains the cliff it came from. count is how many are CONSIDERED; each survivor is a draw call. `chokedSegment` gets a heavy extra pile: that is the chamber choked with fallen rock.
path._ridgeNote_apron: THE LIP IS THE CONTAINMENT ARGUMENT. Everything else in the plan drifts along the journey — width, centreline, the ridge's own height — and a drifting wall beside a floor is a staircase: the grade you feel standing still is the wall's slope times how fast the wall moves, and there is always somewhere that product falls under player.maxClimbGrade. A flood fill found three separate versions of that route, each time creeping a couple of metres up the ridge and then traversing the flank for two kilometres over the top of every one-way drop on the path. ridgeLip closes it by being a DISCONTINUITY: the ground jumps this many metres the instant you pass the floor's edge, so the grade of that step is ridgeLip/stride whatever the stride is, and the smaller the step the more steeply it is refused. Nothing that drifts can soften a discontinuity. It also reads as what it is — a scoured slot where the floor meets the wall at a break rather than a slope. Do not replace it with a talus apron; a linear apron is exactly the thing that failed.

sky._note: The sky gradient, baked into the sky shader at load. Triples are r,g,b in 0..1. 'haze' should stay close to render.fogColour — that match is what makes the ground fade into the sky instead of ending at a visible line. 'dither' hides banding in the gradient on 8-bit screens; set it to 0 to switch that off.
sky._note_glare: glareDepthTest: true means terrain hides the sun's glare, which is what you want in a canyon. Set false for the old open-plain behaviour where the glare always showed.

climate._note: The whole clock. dawn0 is where the dawn line starts in metres; dawnVelocity is metres per second. lethal is the temperature that kills a site. THE BAND. The survivable window is bounded on BOTH sides and both bounds are set here: ground more than (lethal+lethalMargin)/k metres behind the dawn line is lost, and ground more than (coldDamageThreshold-baseTemp)/nightSlope metres ahead of it starts costing suit integrity. With k=0.116 and nightSlope=0.051 that is about 550 m each way — a 1100 m window sweeping a 2510 m corridor at dawnVelocity, so the player is genuinely pinned inside a moving band rather than free to run to the far end and wait. The prologue is walked with the clock frozen, so dawn0 must place that window over the whole stretch from spawn to the handover camp.
climate._graceNote: THE GRACE PERIOD. Mission time (S.t) does not advance until the clock starts, and until it does the dawn line does not move, no ground heats and nothing can be lost — every function in climate.js is a pure function of t and is simply handed a t that is not going anywhere. The world is not frozen, only the clock: grass, wind, gait, dust and the soundfield all ride S.animT, which runs from the first frame. backstopSeconds is the safety net for a player who never trips the story trigger; set it to 0 to remove the net entirely, in which case the clock only ever starts from the story. See src/game/clock.js.
climate._shadeNote: Shade is survival. Ground the west wall hides from the sun heats at (1 - shadeRelief) of the open rate, so it stays under the lethal line far longer — that shaded stripe is the only ground worth standing on once the dawn line has gone past. samples/stepMetres are the ray march toward the sun: samples*stepMetres must reach past the far wall or distant shadow is missed. softnessMetres is how many metres of penumbra the shadow edge gets instead of a hard line.

player._climbNote: maxClimbGrade is the steepest ground the suit will take, as a rise over run: 0.8 is about 39 degrees. The canyon walls are far steeper than this, which is what keeps you in the canyon — there is no invisible wall anywhere in this game.

hands._note: The first-person arms. rest* is arms down (barely out of frame); raise* is the scanner held up while surveying. Angles are radians: bigger shoulder swings the whole arm forward, bigger elbow folds the forearm up. leftBias and leftRaiseShare keep the two arms from being mirror images, which is what made them look wrong.

gait._note: The elbow base bend of 0.30 rad is load-bearing. A straight arm reads as a robot. gait.test.js asserts it never goes below this.

colour._note: Blade colour. 'tint' is the per-blade base (multiplied by a random 0.72-1.22 so no two blades match); 'root' is what the bottom of each blade is multiplied by, which is what gives the band depth instead of reading as flat green paper. 'rootHeight' is how far up the blade the root colour has faded out (0..1).

striders._note: The herd walks the CORRIDOR. bandOffset is how far ahead of (positive) or behind (negative) the dawn line the middle of the herd stays — they follow the grass, which is at grass.bandOffset, so keep the two near each other. spreadX is how far the herd strings out along the journey; lateralFraction is how much of the corridor's half-width they use across it, so they fit a 28 m pass and a 80 m chamber without any per-place tuning. THEY ARE GOING THE SAME WAY YOU ARE, for the same reason. That is the whole point: the biosphere is surveyed by catching up to them, not by crossing them. audibleRange and closeRange feed the soundfield strip, which is how you know whether they are ahead or behind you in a corridor where you cannot see past the next pass.
striders._note_bandOffset: Metres from the dawn line to the middle of the herd. POSITIVE IS AHEAD OF THE LINE, which is where animals that have to outrun a burn actually walk. It used to be negative, which put the whole herd inside the fire. At 200 they come up the trail behind you shortly after the handover, overtake you, and lead for the rest of the run: measured, a walker who stops to survey has them ahead for 71% of the journey. Raising it past about 380 puts them ahead at the handover itself, and that costs the walker a finding — the biosphere window closes too early. Do not move it without running npm run balance.

ashwaiters._note: Currently a damage radius, not a creature. Known issue 2 in HANDOFF.

sites._note: The six findings. Prose for each lives in story.json under the same id. duration is seconds of holding still to complete the survey. THE FIVE STATIC FINDINGS SIT AT THE HEAD OF A POCKET — a detour off the main line, named in terrain.path.segments[].pocket.gives. The main line is safe forward progress; reaching a finding costs the walk out and the walk back, and the dawn charges for both. bio still has followsBand and is the one exception; phase 3 puts it on the herd.
sites._durationNote: duration is how long a survey takes, in seconds, and it is the ONE cost the player cannot buy their way out of by sprinting. The arithmetic, because it is not obvious: a detour's walking cost scales with 1/speed, so sprint (9 m/s) pays 2.14x less for it than walk (4.2 m/s) — which means no amount of geometry can stop a sprinter taking every finding. Survey time is speed-neutral, so it is the only lever that makes the choice a choice. For a sprinter to be unable to take all six while a walker can still take two or three, duration has to exceed roughly (run - mainLine/sprint - allDetours/sprint) / 4. These were 3 seconds, which was a placeholder; run npm run balance after changing them and read the 'how many of the six' line rather than guessing.
sites._bioNote: bio is the biosphere and it is the one finding that MOVES: it is surveyed by catching up to the herd, whose x is pinned to the dawn line by striders.bandOffset. followsBand still means 'this objective is wherever the herd is', but it no longer means 'never lost'. The herd walks forward at the same speed as the dawn and eventually walks out past the far end of the path, and that is a real deadline the manifest counts down to — see manifest.bandDeadline(). striders.reachAtEnd is how close to the head of the path a survey can still be taken from.

camps._note: Only camp five is here. The Meridian moved across the planet for forty years, so camps one to four are somewhere else on this world and exist only in the record; their findings are recovered from the relay archive at the shelter — see shelter.archive. grantsSurvey is the one that matters: the camp carrying Vantaa's final entry is where the six findings are handed over, and reading it is what puts them on the manifest and starts the clock. Before it there is no manifest and nothing is expiring. Exactly one camp should carry this flag, and it must be one the player can actually reach.

graves._note: Only the deaths from the years they had stopped moving are buried here: raman (24), ruiz (31), vantaa (41). Okonkwo (9) and Demir (17) died while the survey was still travelling and are buried somewhere the player will never go. Their records still exist in story.json — that is where the answer key comes from — but their plates are not in this world, so nothing here states the year they died. g4 MOVED from x=-62 to x=-100 in the earned-manifest pass: at -62 it sat 6 m from the shortest walkable line between spawn and camp five, well inside its own 16 m read radius, so the player read it by walking past rather than by choosing to look. At -100 the walk passes 44 m away — 28 m clear of the radius — while the cairn stays in unobstructed line of sight from 71% of that walk. Seeing a marker and deciding to go to it is the whole point of an unmarked grave; being handed it is not.

shelter._note: The sixth camp. Only appears on the compass after camp five is read, and then only as '?'.
shelter._archiveNote: The relay terminal held everything the survey ever filed, because Lindqvist ran the relay. Each pair is [finding, which camp's record describes it] — the gift text is that camp's own line from story.json, so nothing new is written. Camp five carries the final entry and nothing else; loading four findings onto that beat would bury it.

chart._note: The chart is drawn as ink, not as filled squares: contour lines and hachures (the short downhill strokes ruled across a slope) carry the elevation, and everything unwalked is left blank. 'wobble' numbers are how unsteady the hand is, in pixels — 0 everywhere gives a clean drafted chart, higher gives a rougher field sketch. Nothing here is random: the same chart always draws the same way, so the PNG you export is the chart you were looking at.

palette._note: Ink on ground. Swap 'ground' for a pale paper tone and the ink colours for dark ones if you ever want it to read as paper rather than as a field display.

compass._note_labels: labelGapPx: minimum pixels between two compass labels. When sites cluster on one bearing, the nearer one keeps its text and the others show only an arrow.
compass._note_bed: The soundfield strip's idle level. It is not idle any more: the bars are the floor of the three ambient beds, so the strip empties as you walk out of the growth and into the burn and fills again under a closed canopy. bedFloor is what you get with nothing around you at all. The ashwaiter null multiplies the whole thing, so full null is a flat line — that is the point.

deduction._note: The Meridian worksheet. minPerCommit is how many fates must be entered before the record will accept them — the point of it being more than one is that a player cannot test a single guess at a time and walk the answer out of the game. Three is the Obra Dinn number.
deduction._openingNote: openingGrave is the marker you land beside. Reading it fills that one row of the worksheet and leaves the other five empty. Nothing says anything about it — one filled row against five blank ones is the whole of the communication. Set it to null and the game starts with an empty sheet instead.
deduction._datesNote: datesFromRecord is the switch for the two crew whose graves are not in this world. Okonkwo (year 9) and Demir (year 17) died while the survey was still travelling, and NOTHING readable in this crevice states either year — the only place those dates appear is on their plates, which are elsewhere. So the worksheet cannot currently be completed for them, and it should not offer dates the player has no evidence for. Put the grave record ids here (e.g. ["g1","g2"]) ONLY once a log the player can actually reach states those years; the dates then become selectable when the shelter is read. Empty is the honest state until then.

textures._note: Every texture is drawn in code at load — there are no image files. Sizes are pixels per side: a 512 map costs about 1.4 MB on the graphics card, a 256 map about 350 KB. If the game runs slowly it halves all of these automatically (render.downgrade.textureScale) and redraws them. Setting 'enabled' false turns every generated map off and falls back to plain colours.

audio._note: Everything you hear is made from filtered noise at run time — there are no sound files. Gains are 0..1 and they add up, so raising several at once is how you get distortion. FOUR BEDS now, and they are the jungle: 'wind' is the canopy moving over your head, 'insects' is the stridulating mass in the growth around you, 'water' is what is standing in the low ground, and 'herd' is the animals ahead of you on the trail. All four pass through one duck gain that the ashwaiter null pulls to zero — see 'null'. Mute is V.

smoothing._note: Seconds for a level to travel most of the way to its target. Small is twitchy, large is syrupy. 'null' is deliberately quicker than the rest — the silence should arrive faster than it leaves.

wind._note: THE CANOPY. Not open-sky wind any more: this is air moving through a roof of leaves eighteen metres up, so it is the loudest thing you hear under a closed canopy and it thins out where the canopy breaks. 'gain' is the level with no canopy at all; canopyGain is what a fully closed roof adds. Elevation and heat still add to it. Gusts are two slow sines beating against each other so the bed never loops audibly.

herd._note: THE HERD, AHEAD OF YOU ON THE TRAIL. They trampled this path ninety days ago and they are walking it again now, in front of you, and the only way to know how far is to listen. Three cues, and they are all distance: level (curve above 1 keeps them felt rather than heard until you are close), brightness (lowpassSpreadHz opens up as you close, so far away is a rumble and near is hooves), and pulse — inside 'pulseFrom' metres the mass starts to come apart into individual animals. behindLowpassMul is the one cue that is direction rather than distance: a stereo panner cannot separate dead-ahead from dead-behind, but muffling can. Range comes from striders.audibleRange.

foot._note: One burst per footfall, fired off the gait phase so it lands with the foot rather than on a timer. 1.3g is in these numbers: low filter, slow decay, weight. 'phaseOffset' slides the hit earlier or later in the stride.

null._note: The ashwaiter silence. At full null everything is multiplied by zero — actual silence, not a quiet mix. 'curve' above 1 makes the drop bite earlier as you approach the den.

insects._note: THE INSECTS. The floor of a jungle soundfield and the one bed that tells you where you are in the day: they are silent ahead of the growth, deafening in it, and they go out as it browns. Level is jungle.growthAt (the same curve the plants are drawn with) times the local canopy, so a break in the roof is quieter as well as hotter. 'stridulateRate' is the tremolo in Hz — a mass of animals rubbing, not one — and 'stridulateDepth' is how much of the level it swings. Band-passed high and narrow, which is what makes it read as insects and not as hiss.

water._note: THE WATER. Water arrives at dawn, so there is standing water in every hollow behind the line. Level is jungle.wetnessAt — the same test the ponds are placed by — so you hear it exactly where it is. Band-passed mid-high with a little movement on the filter, which is as close to running water as filtered noise gets.

timing._note: fleetTransmissionDelayMs is measured from the moment the briefing's naming beat closes and the player steps outside — WALL clock, not mission time, so it fires whether or not the survey has been handed over yet. At 120000 (two minutes) it lands at about the point a player who walked straight to camp five is reading Vantaa's last entry, which may or may not be where it belongs. It is a placeholder block (story.fleetTransmission) and this is the one number that decides when it arrives.

render._lightNote: One warm key (the fixed low sun) and two cool fills. Keeping the key warm and the fills cool is what gives the ground shape; making them the same colour flattens it.

downgrade._note: Keep this path working. Target is 60fps on integrated graphics.

render._fogNote: THE FOG IS THE PERFORMANCE BUDGET. THREE.FogExp2 fades as 1 - exp(-(density*depth)^2), so transmittance is 5% at 1.73/density metres and 1% at 2.15/density. At 0.055 that is 31 m and 39 m: the sightline the jungle wants, and the reason this runs faster than the rock corridor did rather than slower. camera.far follows it down — drawing past the fog is drawing nothing — and so does shadowCameraExtent, because a shadow you cannot see through the fog is a shadow map you did not need.

mobile._note: What a phone starts at, applied immediately instead of waiting to measure a stutter the player has already seen. These are RENDER-ONLY reductions: the world is still generated in full, so a phone and a desktop see the same rocks in the same places — only fewer of them are drawn. Set 'force' to true or false to override the automatic detection while testing on a desktop.

stick._note: The left thumb stick. radius is how far from where you first touched counts as full deflection; sprintAt is the fraction of that travel where walking becomes sprinting, because there is no shift key on a phone. deadZone stops a resting thumb from drifting.

props._note: Water and frost surfaces. water.depth is how far the surface sits above the LOWEST ground inside its radius — raise it and the pool spreads and deepens, lower it and it shrinks to nothing. frost.lift is how far the sheet floats above the ground it lies on.

jungle._note:
THE JUNGLE. Everything that fills the trail, and all of it INSTANCED — one draw call per layer, not one per plant. Five layers, each a count and a size range:
  canopy      the roof. Wide low-poly crowns on tall stems, thickest where the path.segments canopy value is high and absent where it breaks.
  trunk       what holds the canopy up. Tapered columns, leaning.
  understory  the WALL. Dense mid-height mass standing on the bank at the trail's edge; this is what the player reads as impassable, and it is why the containment bank underneath only has to be a couple of metres tall.
  fern        knee-to-chest growth spilling onto the trail itself.
  litter      fallen fronds and debris flat on the ground.
GROWTH STATE is not baked. Every layer's vertex shader is handed the dawn line's position each frame and scales and tints each instance by how far behind that line it stands: still coming up ahead of it, full at it, browning behind it, black in the burn. One uniform a frame; the GPU does the rest. growthRise/growthFull/growthBurn are those distances in metres BEHIND the dawn line.
THE CANOPY IS THE SHADE MECHANIC. A rock wall cannot shade a corridor whose sun sits at +x along it, but a roof can. terrain.shadeAt returns the greater of the terrain's own occlusion and the canopy's, and climate.js is untouched — it takes occlusion as a parameter and always did. gapFrequency/gapDepth are the holes in the roof: where the canopy breaks the sun gets in and that ground cooks on schedule.
jungle._growthNote: Distances in metres behind the dawn line. Ahead of it (negative) the growth has not come up: scaled down to growthMinScale. From the line back to growthFull it is at full height and greenest. From growthFull back to growthBurn it browns. Past growthBurn it is in the burn: black, collapsed, and the ground there is already lethal.
jungle._canopyNote: How the roof turns into occlusion. `canopy` on each path segment is the cover over the TRAIL, which is the thinnest cover anywhere: the herd breaks the growth down along it every ninety days, so the roof there is torn and the sun gets in. offBoost is how much more cover you get by stepping off the trail into growth nothing has walked through, reaching its full extra by offFull metres out. That gradient is doing real work — it makes the DETOURS the shaded places and the main line the exposed one, so safe forward progress is also hot progress. The gap field then punches holes in whatever is left, so a nominally closed stretch still has sun coming through in places. gapDepth is how deep those holes go.
jungle._waterNote: Water arrives at dawn, so the low ground is wet. Standing water is an instanced flat quad wherever the trail's own floor sits more than `pondBelow` metres under the local mean; streams run the length of the trail's lowest line.
jungle._meshNote: EVERY LAYER IS ONE DRAW CALL. 26k plants in six InstancedMeshes, against 598 individually-drawn rocks before this pass and 300 after it. If you raise a count, you are buying instances, not draw calls — that is the trade this module exists to make.
jungle._note_growth: WHERE THE ONE DAY SITS, in metres BEHIND the dawn line. Negative is ahead of it. These have to be set against where the player actually STANDS relative to that line, which is not obvious: the lethal edge trails the dawn line by about 550 m, so a player running from the heat spends the whole timed run somewhere between 380 m ahead of the line and a few hundred behind it, depending entirely on how much they stop to survey. growthRise was -90 at first, which put the entire visible world inside the 18% stubble zone for anyone who kept walking. At -1000 the growth comes up across the player's whole range instead: young and thin ahead of them, full right behind the line, browning after growthFull, black by growthBurn — which lands in the same place the ground turns lethal. Sprint hard enough and you outrun the growth into bare ground, which is real and is meant to be.

_note_buildStamp: Shown small under the manifest. Bump this on every push — if the game on screen shows an older stamp than the newest push, the browser is serving a cached copy.
